chunks: When SoC accuracy matters most. The question: When it SoC measurement accuracy more desired? When does it not matter as much?
How accurate a battery gauge needs to be depends on what happens if it is wrong. If the error could crash a drone or cost a lot of money, you need a precise gauge.
If the worst case is a cheap flashlight dimming a bit early, a simple voltage check is enough. The goal is the cheapest method that is good enough for the job.
Compare the fuel gauge on a lawnmower with the one on an airliner. If the lawnmower gauge is off, you walk to a gas can.
If the airliner gauge is off, the stakes are very different, so it gets redundant sensors and careful testing. You spend effort in proportion to what a mistake costs.
Battery gauges follow the same rule.
A simple way to choose the estimator class. The branch is controlled by consequence first, then by how well voltage can serve as a proxy.
In every branch, hard overvoltage/undervoltage/overcurrent protection stays.
State of charge (SoC): how full the battery is, as a percentage ("Determining state of charge and why it's hard"). Voltage-based estimate: guessing SoC from the cell voltage.
It is cheap, but poor in the flat part of the curve and under load. Coulomb counting: adding up current over time to track charge. It works under load but drifts.
Flat region: the middle of the voltage curve, where each 1% of charge changes the voltage by only a few millivolts.
Load profile: how much current the device draws, and whether it comes in short pulses.

"Accuracy matters in proportion to the consequence of being wrong.
It matters most in drones, medical devices, EVs and grid storage, where an error means a crash, a patient at risk, or real money in unused battery.
It matters less in cheap or replaceable products like toys or remotes, where a voltage cutoff protects the cell.
Technically, it also depends on load and where you are on the curve: voltage is fine near empty and light loads, but poor in the flat middle or under pulses."
